981.title: Iraq
981.hook: the Jews of Iraq, descendants of the Babylonian exile, from the rivers of Babylon to the streets of Baghdad
981.howItsDone: Jews of Iraqi descent keep Babylonian Jewish customs and melodies in their synagogues and homes, and Jewish students everywhere study the Babylonian Talmud that took shape in Iraq's academies.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Mimouna, and your line: the front door stays open. Sweets, blessings and neighbors welcome. A new week starts, and it travels east, to the land between two rivers.

"By the rivers of Babylon, there we sat down, yea, we wept, when we remembered Zion." That line from the Psalms is sung by people who have never seen those rivers. But some Jews did not just sing about Babylon. They stayed there. Their families lived beside the Tigris and the Euphrates, in the land we now call Iraq, from the exile onward. Today, a community that began in tears and went on to build something lasting.
screen: `BY THE RIVERS OF BABYLON.` → `SOME STAYED.` → `THE LAND WE CALL IRAQ.`

segments.voice: The Tanakh tells how the Babylonian army destroyed Jerusalem and its Temple and carried many of its people away to Babylon. Psalm one hundred thirty-seven is their grief. But the book of Ezekiel opens in the same land, with a surprise. The prophet is not in the Temple. He is in Babylon, beside a river, and he says so plainly: "as I was among the captives by the river Chebar, that the heavens were opened, and I saw visions of God." The Temple was far away, and the heavens opened anyway. When the Persians later allowed a return to Jerusalem, some went home. Others stayed. That community grew into a great center of Jewish learning. In its academies the rabbis argued and taught for generations, and their discussions became the Babylonian Talmud. So a text studied in yeshivas today was shaped beside the same rivers where the exiles once wept. Later, under the caliphs, Baghdad rose nearby, and Jewish life moved into its streets: scholars, merchants, families, synagogues, and a Judeo-Arabic way of speaking all their own. Then, after hard and frightening years, the community left, much of it for Israel. A very old story, from Babylon to Baghdad, almost closed in one lifetime. Still, its Talmud, its melodies and its recipes go on wherever its children live.
screen: `CARRIED AWAY TO BABYLON.` · `THE HEAVENS OPEN BY THE CHEBAR.` · `THE BABYLONIAN TALMUD.` · then, large: `FROM BABYLON TO BAGHDAD.`

segments.voice: Picture a riverbank, and people sitting there far from home. Then the same riverbank generations later: houses, gardens, a room full of students arguing over a page. Hold both, the grief and the life that grew after it, and if you pray, remember the Jews of Iraq in your own words.
Iraq. The land of ancient Babylon, where Jewish exiles settled, where the Babylonian Talmud took shape, and where Jews later lived in Baghdad. Today's word.
Your line: babylon to baghdad. The heavens opened beside a foreign river. That's day nine hundred eighty-one.

982.title: Persia
982.hook: Jews in Iran since Esther's day, a community that endures
982.howItsDone: Persian Jewish families, in Iran and abroad, keep Persian foods and melodies at Shabbat and holiday tables, read the Esther scroll at Purim, and some visit the tomb in Hamadan that tradition links to Esther and Mordecai.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Iraq, and your line: babylon to baghdad. A community that began in tears and kept on growing. Today, just east of Babylon, the kingdom that ruled it next.

At Purim, Jews read aloud a story set in a Persian palace. A king named Ahasuerus. A queen named Esther who hides that she is Jewish. Her cousin Mordecai at the palace gate. An enemy, Haman, with a plan. Heard from far away, the palace is just a setting. But in the city of Hamadan stands a domed building where, tradition says, Esther and Mordecai are buried, and Persian Jews have visited it for generations. For them, the story is local. Today, Persia.
screen: `A STORY SET IN A PERSIAN PALACE.` → `ESTHER, MORDECAI, HAMAN.` → `A TOMB IN HAMADAN.`

segments.voice: Persia appears all through the later books of the Tanakh, not only in Esther. In Ezra, a Persian king, Cyrus, lets the exiles from Babylon go home and rebuild the Temple. Isaiah goes further, and has God speak to a foreign king by name: "Thus saith the LORD to His anointed, to Cyrus." Daniel serves Persian kings. Nehemiah is cupbearer in the palace at Shushan before he goes to rebuild the walls of Jerusalem. So Persia is the place of both danger and rescue. Haman's plot is hatched there. So is the decree that lets the people return. And not everyone returned. Jewish families stayed in Persia, in Hamadan, Isfahan, Shiraz and other cities, through empire after empire. They spoke Persian and wrote it in Hebrew letters, a language scholars call Judeo-Persian, and copied and translated the Bible in it. Their life was sometimes peaceful and sometimes very hard, with times of forced conversion and times of quiet. Persian Jewish families have also left, to Israel, to the United States, to other places, carrying Persian food, music and Purim customs with them. And a Jewish community still lives in Iran today, with synagogues and schools. That is what the line since Esther means. Not a story about long ago, but a people who stayed in the same land as the story, and are still there.

983.title: Beta Israel
983.hook: Ethiopian Jews, with their own traditions and the festival of Sigd
983.carry: facing a city they have never seen
983.howItsDone: On Sigd, Ethiopian Jews fast, gather on a high place, and listen as the kessim read from the Orit and lead prayers for Jerusalem; in Israel crowds gather on a Jerusalem promenade, and the day ends with a festive meal.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Persia, and your line: since esther. Jews in the land of the story, then and now. Today the map moves south, to the highlands of Ethiopia.

Up a hillside in northern Ethiopia, people in white are walking together. They have been fasting since sunrise. At the front are the priests, the kessim, carrying a sacred book wrapped in bright cloth, under fringed umbrellas. At the top, they turn toward a city none of them has ever seen. Jerusalem. They stand still for a long moment and look out toward it. Today, the Jews of Ethiopia, and the day they climb.
screen: `PEOPLE IN WHITE, FASTING.` → `THE KESSIM AT THE FRONT.` → `FACING JERUSALEM.`

segments.voice: They call themselves Beta Israel, the house of Israel. For a very long time they lived in villages in Ethiopia, cut off from other Jewish communities. Where their story begins, nobody knows for certain. Their own traditions tell more than one account, and scholars argue. What is clear is how they kept their faith. Their Bible, the Orit, is written in Ge'ez, an old Ethiopian language. Their religious leaders are priests called kessim. They kept Shabbat and the laws of purity carefully, without the Talmud that shaped Jewish life elsewhere, so many of their customs grew straight from the text of the Torah. Sigd is their own festival. It comes in the autumn, some weeks after Yom Kippur. People fast, climb a high place, and listen as the kessim read from the Orit. The readings recall the Book of Nehemiah, where, after the return from exile, Ezra the scribe reads the Torah aloud to the gathered people. They bow down with their faces to the ground, then fast, confess, and renew their covenant with God. On Sigd, Beta Israel did the same, and prayed to return to Jerusalem. In the afternoon the fast ends, and everyone comes down the hill to eat and celebrate together. Then the community moved, family by family, to Israel. Now, on Sigd, crowds gather on a promenade in Jerusalem, looking out over the city their grandparents once prayed toward from a hilltop in Ethiopia.

984.title: India
984.hook: three Jewish communities in India: the Bene Israel, the Jews of Cochin, and Baghdadi Jews
984.howItsDone: Bene Israel families keep their own customs, such as the malida offering of flattened rice in honor of Elijah; the Paradesi Synagogue in Kochi still stands, and Jews of Indian descent in Israel and elsewhere keep their communities' songs and foods.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Sigd, and your line: facing a city they have never seen. A covenant renewed from a hilltop. Today, across the Arabian Sea to India, where there is not one Jewish story but three.

In villages along India's western coast, neighbors once had a name for a group of families who pressed oil for a living. They called them the Saturday oil-pressers, because on Saturdays their presses stood still. Nobody worked, nobody lit a fire. The families did not have Torah scrolls or rabbis. What they had, tradition says, was the habit of resting on the seventh day, and one line they never stopped saying. Today, India.
screen: `THE SATURDAY OIL-PRESSERS.` → `THE PRESSES STAND STILL.` → `ONE LINE THEY KEPT.`

segments.voice: The first community is the Bene Israel, the children of Israel. Their own tradition says their ancestors were shipwrecked on the Konkan coast long ago, and lost their books in the sea. They kept what they could: Shabbat, circumcision, some of the festivals, and the Shema. "Hear, O Israel: the LORD our God, the LORD is one." Tradition says they said it at every turn of life. Later, teachers from elsewhere helped them reconnect with the wider Jewish world, and families moved to Bombay. The second community lived on the southwest coast, in Cochin, in Kerala. Cochin Jews were traders along the spice routes. Tradition says a local ruler once gave a Jewish leader named Joseph Rabban copper plates granting rights to his community. In the old quarter of Kochi stands the Paradesi Synagogue, its floor laid with hand-painted blue and white tiles from China, brass lamps hanging above. Cochin Jewish women sang their own songs in Malayalam, the language of Kerala. The third community is the Baghdadi Jews. Yes, Baghdad, from a few days ago. Traders from Iraq and nearby lands settled in Bombay and Calcutta, spoke Arabic and later English, and built synagogues and schools. Three communities, three histories, one country. Since then, families from all three have moved to Israel and elsewhere, and small communities remain. And each of the three, in its own language and its own way, made a home among its neighbors.

India. Home to three Jewish communities: the Bene Israel of the Konkan coast, the Jews of Cochin in Kerala, and the Baghdadi Jews of Bombay and Calcutta. Today's word.

985.title: Kaifeng
985.hook: a Jewish community in China, in the city of Kaifeng on the Yellow River
985.howItsDone: Descendants of Kaifeng's Jews remember their heritage in family memory, and some study Hebrew and Jewish practice today; scholars study the surviving steles and scrolls.

segments.voice: Yesterday, India, and your line: the presses stood still. Three communities in one country. Today, farther east still, to a city on the Yellow River.

A Jesuit priest named Matteo Ricci is living in Beijing when a visitor arrives. The man has heard there are foreigners in the city who worship one God and are not Muslims, and he has come to meet fellow believers. He is from Kaifeng. As they talk, it slowly becomes clear that the visitor is not a Christian at all. He is a Jew, from a community that has lived in China for generations. Neither man had expected the other.
screen: `A VISITOR IN BEIJING.` → `ONE GOD, NOT MUSLIMS.` → `A JEW FROM KAIFENG.`

segments.voice: Kaifeng was once an imperial capital on the Yellow River. Jewish merchants came there, tradition says, along the trade routes from Persia, and stayed. They built a synagogue in a courtyard, Chinese in its architecture, with Torah scrolls inside. They put up stone steles, carved in Chinese, telling their history and their faith in words their neighbors could read. Their neighbors had their own name for them: the religion that plucks out the sinew. That name points straight back to Genesis. After Jacob wrestles through the night and his thigh is touched, the Torah says: "Therefore the children of Israel eat not the sinew of the thigh-vein." The Jews of Kaifeng kept that rule. They removed the sinew from their meat, and the people around them noticed. A practice from a story about Jacob became the name their neighbors called them by. The community had a hard road. The Yellow River flooded, and the synagogue was damaged more than once and rebuilt. Over time, with no new teachers arriving and no rabbis to train, Hebrew faded and the community thinned. The synagogue was eventually gone. Yet some families in Kaifeng still remember that their ancestors were Jews, and some have reconnected with Jewish life. Some of the scrolls and steles survived and are kept in museums and libraries. Kaifeng shows how far a single rule from Genesis could travel, and how long it could be kept.

986.title: The Romaniotes
986.hook: Greek-speaking Jews of Greece, with their own prayers since ancient times
986.howItsDone: Romaniote families gather at the synagogue in Ioannina for summer services and remembrance, and Kehila Kedosha Janina in New York holds services and keeps a small museum of Romaniote life.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Kaifeng, and your line: china. A rule from Genesis, kept far from home. Today the road turns back west, to the mountains of Greece.

In the town of Ioannina, in the mountains of northwestern Greece, a lake sits below an old stone fortress. Inside the walls, down a quiet lane, is a whitewashed synagogue. Most of the year its doors are closed. Then, in summer, families arrive from Athens, from Israel, from New York, and the old benches fill again. Some of the prayers sung there come from a tradition that is neither Sephardic nor Ashkenazi. Today, the Romaniotes.
screen: `A FORTRESS ABOVE A LAKE.` → `A WHITEWASHED SYNAGOGUE.` → `THE BENCHES FILL IN SUMMER.`

segments.voice: The Romaniotes are the Jews of the Greek-speaking world, who lived there long before Jews arrived from Spain. The Tanakh already knows Greece. In the list of nations in Genesis, among the sons of Japheth, is Javan, the Hebrew name for Greece. Romaniote Jews spoke Greek. Some wrote Greek in Hebrew letters, and they had their own prayer book, their own liturgical poems and their own customs. When Jews expelled from Spain arrived in Greek lands, they brought Ladino and Sephardic customs, and in many cities the older Romaniote ways were absorbed into the new. Ioannina was different. There the Romaniote rite held on, and the synagogue inside the fortress kept its old prayers and melodies. The Holocaust reached Ioannina too. Its Jews were rounded up and deported, and few came back. After the war, the community that remained was tiny. But the descendants did not forget. In New York, Romaniote families from Ioannina built their own synagogue, Kehila Kedosha Janina, on the Lower East Side, and it still holds services. In Ioannina, the old synagogue opens for prayer and remembrance, and families return to stand in it. The Romaniotes are a reminder that the map of Jewish life has more than two colors.
screen: `JEWS OF THE GREEK-SPEAKING WORLD.` · `JAVAN, GREECE IN GENESIS.` · `IOANNINA KEEPS THE OLD RITE.` · then, large: `MORE THAN TWO COLORS.`

The Romaniotes. The Greek-speaking Jews of the old eastern Roman world, with their own prayers and poems, whose rite lives on in Ioannina. Today's word.

987.title: Mizrahi Jews
987.hook: a Hebrew word for east gathers the Jews of the Middle East and North Africa
987.howItsDone: Mizrahi Jewish families often keep the prayer customs, melodies and holiday foods of the country their grandparents came from, and sacred Hebrew poems called piyyutim are sung at Shabbat tables and in synagogue.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Romaniotes, and your line: greece. Greek-speaking Jews with their own old rite. Today closes the week with one word for a wide map.

Look back at the road this week has walked. Baghdad, between its two rivers. Persia, and the people of Esther. The Sigd on an Ethiopian hilltop. Jewish streets in India, in Kaifeng, in Greece. Each stop had its own language, its own food, its own way of singing the psalms. Now comes a Hebrew word that gathers some of those homes under one roof, and it works like a compass needle. Today's word is Mizrahi.
screen: `A WEEK OF JOURNEYS.` → `BAGHDAD, PERSIA, INDIA, GREECE.` → `ONE WORD LIKE A COMPASS.`

segments.voice: In Hebrew, mizrah means east, and Mizrahi means eastern. Today the word is used for Jews whose families lived across the Middle East and North Africa: Iraq and Iran, Yemen and Syria, Morocco, Tunisia, Egypt and beyond. Here's the first surprise. It's a newer word than the communities it names. A family in Baghdad or in Fez did not wake up calling itself Mizrahi. It called itself Baghdadi, or Moroccan, or simply Jewish. As the story is usually told, the word came into wide use later, in Israel, where Jews from these lands lived side by side with Jews from Europe. Some people carry the word with pride. Some prefer the name of their own city or country. Some North African Jews also call themselves Sephardi. The point here is to listen to how people name themselves. Now the second surprise, the compass. In some Jewish homes in Europe and America, a decorated plaque hangs on the eastern wall. It's called a mizrah, because from there, Jerusalem lies to the east. But for a family praying in Baghdad, Jerusalem lay to the west. So a Jew in Baghdad, called eastern, turned west to pray, while a Jew in Fez still faced east. The word depends on where you stand. The psalm uses that same compass for something wider: "As far as the east is from the west," so far has God removed our wrongs from us. A distance too wide to measure. And the sound of this word? At a Shabbat table in a Mizrahi home you may hear sacred Hebrew poems sung in melodies that also echo Arabic, Persian or Turkish music. The east, in a song.
screen: `MIZRAH MEANS EAST.` · `A NEWER WORD FOR OLD HOMES.` · `EAST DEPENDS ON WHERE YOU STAND.` · `SACRED POEMS, EASTERN MELODIES.` · then, large: `AS FAR AS THE EAST IS FROM THE WEST.`

segments.voice: If you know a melody from a family table, a psalm or a blessing in an old tune, let it hum quietly in you, without words if you like. If no song comes, listen to the sounds around you, near and far, and let them be the music.
Mizrahi. Eastern, from the Hebrew word for east: a name for Jews of the Middle East and North Africa. Today's word.
Your line: the east. East of where depends on where you stand. Day nine hundred eighty-seven.
